name: Märzen / Oktoberfest
title: Märzen and Oktoberfest: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Märzen and Oktoberfest lager explained: the toasty amber festival beer, how it tastes, how to serve it and Indian dishes to pair.
tagline: Brewed in spring, drunk in autumn: the toasty amber lager behind every Oktoberfest menu.
tastes:
Märzen is named after March, the last month Bavarian brewers could safely brew before summer heat spoiled fermentations. They made it a little stronger, lagered it cold in caves through the summer and drank the last of it in autumn, which is how it became tied to Oktoberfest. Today the name covers a rich amber lager with a lot of Munich and Vienna malt, giving toast, light caramel and a bready sweetness.

It is fuller and a touch stronger than a standard lager, yet it should finish clean and fairly dry so you can drink a litre mug without tiring. Hop bitterness is moderate and German in character, herbal rather than fruity. One wrinkle: the beer served in Munich's festival tents today is usually a paler, lighter festbier, while the deeper amber Märzen survives more in export bottles and in craft breweries abroad. Both share the same idea, malt-led and smooth, built for long sessions with food.

profile.look: Deep gold to amber copper, brilliantly clear, with a dense off-white head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Toasted bread, light caramel and malt sweetness, a clean lager character and a gentle herbal hop note in the background.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium body, smooth and rounded, moderate carbonation, finishing dry enough to invite another sip.
profile.ingredients: Munich and Vienna malts over a pale base, German noble hops such as Hallertau or Tettnang, clean lager yeast, long cold lagering.

in_india: Oktoberfest menus have made Märzen one of the easiest German styles to find in India. Bengaluru brewpubs pour it every September and October, and some Mumbai breweries keep it on their list. That timing works well, as it lands just after the monsoon when the evenings cool a little. A brewpub Märzen should be fresh and clean; if it tastes cardboard-like or sweet and flabby, it has sat too long or warmed in transit. It is a natural choice for a big group lunch.

pairings.why: The beer's malt sweetness softens the vinegar and chilli heat while its body stands up to the fatty pork.
Toasty malt matches the crisp potato and the carbonation lifts the yoghurt and tamarind chutney.
Rich, toasty malt calms the fierce Kolhapuri masala without disappearing under it.
Caramelised gram flour and ghee sit alongside the beer's toasted malt, and the dry finish stops it from cloying.
